messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel is a 48-year-old shopowner who came to treatment more than a year after his wife’s sister died violently, an event he had been pulled into at close range because he was the family member who identified the body and helped make the funeral arrangements. He still describes the day in fragments that are painfully sharp: the funeral home’s fluorescent light, the stillness of her face, the scent of flowers and polished wood, his wife collapsing beside him. What stays with him is not only that she was gone, but the helplessness of being the one who had to look, confirm, and keep functioning while his wife was falling apart. Since then, anything tied to loss has become charged. If a customer in his store starts talking about someone who “lost their mom” or “buried a brother,” Daniel feels his body tense before he can think. Passing a cemetery on the drive to work or hearing about a funeral in town can unsettle him for the rest of the day, and reminders of victims in the news or in conversation hit him with particular force because they pull him back toward the image of his sister-in-law’s body.

What frightened Daniel early on was how suddenly ordinary moments could feel dangerous. A stock cart clattering in the back of the shop or someone stepping into his peripheral vision makes him jolt hard, his chest already braced as if something terrible is about to happen. In those moments the old scene comes back with unnerving force. He does not experience it as a sad memory he is choosing to recall; it is more like the room at the funeral home has opened again around him. The image is vivid and exact, and it replays “like a film,” as he puts it, with details he wishes he could forget. Because he is already on edge, reminders of loss land harder: a grieving customer, a bouquet meant for a memorial, even the word “funeral” seems to leap out at him, and he scans for these cues almost automatically.

Over the months that followed, Daniel built his days around not setting any of this off. In the shop, if conversation turns toward death or bereavement, he finds a reason to walk into the storeroom or abruptly changes the subject. He has stopped attending funerals altogether and will not drive past the cemetery if there is any alternate route. At home, if his wife begins talking about her sister, he goes quiet, lights a cigarette, and steps outside rather than let himself think about that day. The same thing happens when the memory intrudes on its own: he reaches for a cigarette, focuses on small tasks, or pushes the thoughts away as if refusing them will keep him steady. His avoidance makes immediate sense to him because he is convinced that if he lets himself dwell on it, he will be pulled all the way back into those moments and lose control.

But the more Daniel has organized his life around not thinking and not feeling, the less settled he has become. Because he cuts off conversations about loss and steers clear of funerals, cemeteries, and other grief-related reminders, those situations have stayed raw and potent; they still hit him like something current rather than something survived. Pushing the images away has not weakened them. If anything, the memory returns more forcefully, highly detailed and present, especially after days when he has been trying hardest not to think about it. Smoking gives him a brief sense of relief, yet he notices that after stepping outside for a cigarette he often comes back even more tightly wound, more reactive to noise and sudden movement in the store, more likely to be set off by some mention of another family’s loss. On bad days this pattern repeats several times before lunch.

The effect on his life has narrowed him. Daniel used to be the kind of owner who chatted easily with regulars; now his staff have noticed that he disappears when certain conversations start, and his wife experiences him as shut down whenever her sister is mentioned. He hates that, because part of him knows he is leaving her alone with her grief, yet what he feels most strongly is fear—fear of the surge of horror, guilt, and helplessness that comes if he lets the memory come fully into view. He sought help after startling violently when a customer dropped a box near the register and, seconds later, finding himself back in the funeral home so completely that he had to leave the floor. What he wants is not to erase his sister-in-law, but to be able to hear about loss, stand beside his wife, and walk through his own days without feeling as though the worst moment of his life is still happening now.
